readingSections.title: Introduction
readingSections.content: PROFIT & LOSS

readingSections.title: Cost Price
readingSections.content:
This is the amount paid to acquire an item, often referred to as the cost price or CP.

The Cost Price (CP) is not solely the amount spent to purchase an item. It also includes any additional expenses incurred before selling the item.

For instance, if Raman buys a used bicycle for Rs 2000 and spends Rs 500 on its maintenance before selling it, the cost price will be the total of the purchase price and the maintenance cost.

Therefore, CP = Purchase Price + Maintenance Cost. In this case,

$$CP = 2000 + 500 = 2500.$$

readingSections.title: Selling Price
readingSections.content:
The selling price, or SP, is the amount received when an item is sold.

The difference between the cost price and the selling price determines whether a profit or loss has been made. A profit is realized when the selling price exceeds the cost price, while a loss occurs when the selling price is less than the cost price. In the case of profit and loss percentage cost price is the base value and if we calculate in percentage then in the case of profit and loss cost price is generally considered as 100%.

readingSections.title: Profit (P)
readingSections.content:
Profit arises when the selling price of an item exceeds its purchase price. It can be calculated using the formula:

$$Profit = Selling Price - Cost Price$$

By using the percentage formula

$$Profit \% = \frac{Profit}{Cost price} \times 100\% = \frac{SP - CP}{CP} \times 100\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 1
readingSections.content:
Anjali purchased a laptop for Rs 45000 and sold it to a customer for Rs 60000. Find her profit percentage.

### Solution

readingSections.title: Calculate the Profit
readingSections.content:
Profit = Selling Price - Cost Price

Profit = Rs 60000 (Selling Price) - Rs 45000 (Cost Price) = Rs 15000

readingSections.title: Calculate the Profit Percentage
readingSections.content:
$$Profit\ Percentage = \frac{Profit}{Cost\ price} \times 100$$

$$Profit\ Percentage = \frac{15000}{45000} \times 100 = 33.33\%$$

Therefore, Anjali made a profit of 33.33% on the sale of the laptop.

readingSections.title: Loss (L)
readingSections.content:
A loss is experienced when the cost incurred to acquire an item surpasses the amount received from its sale. It can be calculated using the formula:

$$Loss = Cost\ Price - Selling\ Price$$

By using the percentage formula

$$Loss \% = \frac{Loss}{Cost\ Price} \times 100\% = \frac{CP - SP}{CP} \times 100\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 2
readingSections.content:
Jordan bought a second-hand car for Rs 1,000,000 and invested Rs 200,000 in its maintenance. If Jordan had to sell it for Rs 900,000, then find his loss percentage.

### Solution

Total cost = Rs 1,000,000 + Rs 200,000 = Rs 1,200,000.

He sold the car for Rs 900,000.

So, his loss is Rs 1,200,000 - Rs 900,000 = Rs 300,000.

$$\text{Loss}\% = \frac{\text{Loss}}{\text{Total Cost price}} \times 100.$$

Therefore, the loss percentage = $\frac{300000}{1200000} \times 100 = 25\%$.

So, Jordan incurred a loss of 25% on this transaction.

readingSections.title: Example 3
readingSections.content:
Deepa bought a second-hand house for Rs 2,000,000 and invested Rs 500,000 in its maintenance. She also spent Rs 1,000 daily cleaning the house for 25 days and paid a one-time tax of Rs 100,000. If Deepa sold the house for Rs 3,000,000 after 25 days, then find her profit percentage.

### Solution

Total cost = Rs 2,000,000 (purchase price) + Rs 500,000 (maintenance) + Rs 1,000 × 25 (cleaning) + Rs 100,000 (tax) = Rs 2,625,000.

She sold the house for Rs 3,000,000.

So, her profit is Rs 3,000,000 - Rs 2,625,000 = Rs 375,000.

$$\text{Profit}\% = \frac{\text{Profit}}{\text{Total Cost price}} \times 100.$$

Therefore, the profit percentage = $\frac{375,000}{2,625,000} \times 100 =$ approximately 14.29%.

So, Deepa made a profit of 14.29% on this transaction.

readingSections.title: Example 4
readingSections.content:
If Ram bought an item for Rs 840 and sold it at a profit of 40%, what would be the selling price of the item?

### Solution

Ram bought an item for Rs 840 (this is the CP) and sold it at a profit of 40% (this is P).

Substituting these values into the formula gives:

$$SP = 840 \times (100 + 40) \% = 840 \times \frac{140}{100} = \text{Rs } 1176$$

readingSections.title: b) By Percentage
readingSections.content:
When we analyze the relationship between cost price (CP) and selling price (SP) in terms of percentages, we consider the cost price as 100%.

In the case of profit, the profit percentage is added to the 100% (CP). This gives us the selling price as a percentage. For example, if an item is bought at a cost price considered

100% and sold with a profit of 20%,

Then the selling price would be 100% (CP) + 20% (profit) = 120%.

In the case of a loss, the loss percentage is subtracted from the 100% (CP). This gives us the selling price as a percentage. For instance, if an item is bought at a cost price considered 100% and sold with a loss of 10%,

Then the selling price would be 100% (CP) - 10% (loss) = 90%.

readingSections.title: Example 5
readingSections.content:
Rahul loses 8% while selling a book at Rs 644 then find the cost price of the book.

### Solution

The selling price of the book is given as Rs 644.

The selling price represents 92% of the cost price, as it includes an 8% loss from the cost price (100% - 8% = 92%).

We are required to find the original cost price, which is 100%.

To do this, we use the formula:

$$\text{Cost Price} = \frac{\text{Selling Price}}{\text{Selling Price } \%} \times 100\%$$

Substituting the given values into the formula, we get Cost

$$\text{Price} = \frac{644}{92\%} \times 100\% = \text{Rs } 700.$$

Therefore, the original cost price of the book is **Rs 700**.

readingSections.title: c) By fraction
readingSections.content:
**Identify the Base Value (Cost Price):** In profit and loss problems, the base value or denominator is the cost price. This is the price at which an item was originally bought.

**Identify the Percentage Value:** The numerator is the value given in percentage. This could be the profit, loss, or selling price incurred.

**Convert Percentage to Fraction:** Convert the given percentage into a fraction to simplify calculations.

For example, if it's said that there is a 33.33% profit, this can be represented as $\frac{1}{3}$. Here, the profit (1 unit) is a third of the cost price (3 units).

Similarly, if it's said that the selling price is 125%, this can be represented as $\frac{5}{4}$. In this case, the selling price (5 units) is 1.25 times the cost price (4 units).

**Calculate:** Use these values to calculate profit, loss, selling price, etc., as required by the problem as a like ratio.

readingSections.title: Example 6
readingSections.content:
Radha gets 16.66% profit if sells an article at Rs 343 and then finds its purchased price.

### Solution

16.66% profit is represented as $\frac{1}{6}$.

So, the profit (P) is 1 unit and the cost price (CP) is 6 units.

Selling Price (SP) = CP + P = 6 units (CP) + 1 unit (P) = 7 units.

Purchase Price = Cost Price in units × Value of each unit

$$= \frac{343 \times 6}{7} = \text{Rs } 294$$

So, the purchase price of the item is Rs 294.

readingSections.title: Example 7
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper sold an item for Rs 7821, incurring a loss of 21%. What would be the selling price of the item if the shopkeeper wanted to make a profit of 31%?

### Solution

In case of a loss of 21% the selling price = Rs 7821

In case of a loss of 21% the selling price in percentage= (100-21) %=79%

Selling price at 31% profit = (100+31) %=131%

Selling price in case of 31% profit = $\frac{7821}{79\%} \times 131\%$ = Rs 12969

readingSections.title: Example 8
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper mistakenly calculates his profit based on the selling price, and it turns out to be 60%. What is his actual profit percentage?

### Solution

Method 1: Convert the given percentage (60%) into a fraction. This gives us $\frac{3}{5}$.

Assume that the selling price (SP) is 5 units since the profit was calculated based on this.

The profit (P) is then 3 units, as per the fraction we obtained earlier.

To find the cost price (CP), subtract the profit from the selling price. This gives us CP = SP - P = 5 - 3 = 2 units.

Finally, calculate the actual profit percentage using the formula

$$(\frac{P}{CP}) \times 100\% = \frac{3}{2} \times 100\% = 150\%.$$

So, the actual profit percentage is 150%.

Method 2: Let the selling price be Rs. x.

Profit = 60% of Selling Price = 60% of x = 0.6x

We know that,

C.P. = S.P. – Profit

$$C.P. = x - 0.6x = 0.4x$$

Actual Profit % = $\frac{\text{Profit}}{\text{C.P.}} \times 100 = \frac{0.6x}{0.4x} \times 100 = 150\%$

### Method 3

Short trick: When calculating profit, replace the denominator of the fraction with the difference between the numerator and the denominator. Then, convert this value into a percentage.

With a fraction 60% = 3/5, the difference between the denominator and the numerator is 5-3=2

So, profit % = $\frac{3}{5-3} \times 100\% = \frac{3}{2} \times 100\% = 150\%$

readingSections.title: Example 9
readingSections.content:
Ram calculated his profit or loss percentage on selling price and hence incurred a loss of 20% in the transaction. Find his actual loss percentage on cost price?

### Solution

Loss % on S.P. = 20% = $\frac{1}{5}$ S.P. = 5 and Loss = 1

$$CP = S.P. + \text{Loss} = 5 + 1 = 6$$

Loss % on C.P. = $\frac{1}{6} \times 100 = 16\frac{2}{3}\%$

readingSections.title: Price Reduction Allows For Additional Purchases
readingSections.content:
"When a price reduction of 'a%' allows for the purchase of an additional quantity 'c' of items within the same budget 'b',

The reduced price = a% of $\frac{b}{c}$

The Original price = $\frac{ab}{c \times (100 - a)}$

Can be used 1 instead of 100 when using the fraction value of "a". Means,

The reduced price = a of $\frac{b}{c}$

The Original price = $\frac{ab}{c \times (1 - a)}$

readingSections.title: Example 10
readingSections.content:
The price of apple is decreased by 75% so that Ram can purchase 15 kg more in Rs 400, find the reduced price of apple.

### Solution

### Method - 1

Price reduction, a = 75%, Additional quantity, c = 15 kg, Budget, b = Rs 400

95

The reduced price according to the formula is a% of $\frac{b}{c}$

$$\text{Reduced price} = 75\% \text{ of } \frac{400}{15} = 0.75 \times \frac{400}{15} = 20 \text{ Rs/kg}$$

So, the reduced price of apples is 20 Rs/kg.

### Method - 2

$$\text{Price reduction is } 75\% = \frac{75}{100} = \frac{3}{4} = \frac{4-3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}$$

Price is changed in ratio 4 : 1

Relation of price and quantity is inverse if expense is constant (unchanged)

So quantity is changed from 1 : 4 , you can see 3 ratio is increased

According to questions,

$$3 \text{ ratio} = 15 \text{ kg then } 1 \text{ ratio} = \frac{15}{3} = 5 \text{ kg}$$

Increased Quantity of apple 4 ratio = 4 × 5 = 20 kg

$$\text{Price per kg} = \frac{400}{20} = 20 \text{ Rs./kg}$$

readingSections.title: Example 11
readingSections.content:
The price of mango is decreased by 66.66% so that Ram can purchase 50 Kg more for Rs 1500; find the original price of mango.

### Solution

### Method 1

$$\text{Price reduction, a} = 66.66\% = \frac{2}{3}$$

Additional quantity, c = 50 kg

Budget, b = Rs 1500

The original price according to the formula

$$= \frac{ab}{c \times (1-a)}$$

$$\text{Original price} = \frac{\frac{2}{3} \times 1500}{50 \times \left(1 - \frac{2}{3}\right)} = \frac{1000}{50 \times \frac{1}{3}} = 60 \text{ Rs/kg}$$

So, the original price of mango is 60 Rs/kg.

### Method 2

$$\text{Price reduction is } 66.66\% = \frac{2}{3} = \frac{3-2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$$

Price changed in ratio 3 : 1

Relation of price and quantity is inverse if expense is constant (unchanged)

So quantity is changed from 1 : 3 , you can see 2 ratio is increased

According to question,

$$2 \text{ ratio} = 50 \text{ kg then } 1 \text{ ratio } \frac{50}{2} = 25 \text{ kg}$$

Original volume of mango 1 ratio = 25 kg

$$\text{Price per kg} = \frac{1500}{25} = 60 \text{ Rs./kg}$$

readingSections.title: When the Cost Price is equal to the Percentage of Profit or Loss
readingSections.content:
When the numerical value of the profit percentage is equal to the cost price, the relationship between the Selling Price (SP) and Cost Price (CP), or Profit, is given by the following equation

$$CP = \text{Profit}\% = -50 + 10 \sqrt{25 + SP}$$

When the numerical value of the loss percentage is equal to the cost price, the relationship between the Selling Price (SP) and Cost Price (CP), or Loss, is given by the following equation

$$CP = \text{Loss}\% = 50 \pm 10 \sqrt{25 - SP}$$

readingSections.title: Example 12
readingSections.content:
On selling an article at Rs 11, what profit will occur by a shopkeeper if the profit percent is equal to its cost price?

### Solution

**Method 1:** Given the equation  $CP = \text{Profit}\% = -50 + 10 \sqrt{25 + SP}$ , and the selling price (SP) is Rs 11.

$$CP = \text{Profit}\% = -50 + 10 \sqrt{25 + 11} = -50 + 10 \sqrt{36} = -50 + 60 = 10$$

### Method 2

**Short Trick:** Find two factors of the selling price (SP) that have a difference of 10. Then, append a zero to the end of the smaller value. Please note, this is only applicable when the difference between the factors is 10.

The two factors of 11, which have a difference of 10, are 1 and 11.

Append a zero to the smaller value 1 to get 10.

readingSections.title: Example 13
readingSections.content:
On selling an article at Rs 16, what % loss will occur by a shopkeeper if the loss percent is equal to its cost price?

### Solution

**Method 1:** Given the equation  $CP = \text{Loss}\% = 50 \pm 10 \sqrt{25 - SP}$ , and the selling price (SP) is Rs 16.

$$CP = \text{Loss}\% = 50 \pm 10\sqrt{25 - SP} = 50 \pm 10\sqrt{25 - 16} = 50 \pm 30 = 80,20 \text{ (Both are answer)}$$

### Method 2

**Short Trick:** Find two factors of the selling price (SP) that have a sum of 10. Then, append a zero to the end of the both values. Please note, this is only applicable when the sum of the factors is 10.

The two factors of 16, which have a sum of 10, are 8 and 2.

Append a zero to both values of 80 to get 20.

readingSections.title: Example 14
readingSections.content:
If an article is sold for Rs 21, what percentage loss will a shopkeeper incur if the loss percentage is equal to its cost price?

### Solution

**Method 1:** Given the equation $CP = \text{Loss}\% = 50 \pm 10\sqrt{25 - SP}$, where the selling price (SP) is Rs 21.

$$CP = \text{Loss}\% = 50 \pm 10\sqrt{25 - 21} = 50 \pm 10\sqrt{25 - 21} = 50 \pm 20 = 70,30$$

So, the cost price and the loss percentage are both 70 and 30

### Method 2

**Short Trick:** Find two factors of the selling price (SP) that have a sum of 10. Then, append a zero to the end of both values. Please note, this is only applicable when the sum of the factors is 10.

The two factors of 21, which have a sum of 10, are 7 and 3.

Appending a zero to both values gives us 70 and 30.

readingSections.title: When Only Number of Purchased And Sold Item is Given
readingSections.content:
If the number of “a” articles is purchased and the same number of “b” articles is sold at the same price, then the Profit or Loss percentage can be calculated as follows:

$$\text{Profit or Loss } \% = \frac{(a - b)}{b} \times 100\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 15
readingSections.content:
The cost price of 25 articles is equal to the selling price of 15 articles. Find his profit or loss percentage.

### Solution

### Method 1

We can use these values in our formula:

$$\text{Profit or Loss } \% = \frac{(a - b)}{b} \times 100\%$$

By substituting $a = 25$ and $b = 15$ into the formula,

$$\text{We get: Profit } \% = \frac{(25 - 15)}{15} \times 100\% = \frac{10}{15} \times 100\% = 66.67\%$$

So, there is a profit of approximately 66.67% in this transaction.

### Method 2

Let him purchase 25 articles in x Rs.

And he sells 15 articles at x Rs.

So, he has the profit of $25 - 15 = 10$ articles

$$\text{So profit } \% = \frac{10}{15} \times 100 = 66.66\%$$

(Profit or loss in articles always divided by items going out from the shop)

readingSections.title: Example 16
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper sells 21 articles and makes a profit equivalent to the selling price of 6 articles. Find his profit or loss percentage.

### Solution

$$\text{Profit } \% = \frac{\text{Profit}}{\text{Cost Price}} \times 100\%$$

Assume that the selling price of 1 article is Rs 1;

The total selling price for 21 articles is Rs 21.

The profit is equivalent to the selling price of 6 articles, which is Rs 6.

Therefore, the cost price of the 21 articles is Rs 15 (Rs 21 - Rs 6).

Substituting these values into the formula, we get:

$$\text{Profit } \% = \frac{6}{15} \times 100 = 40\%$$

So, the shopkeeper’s profit percentage is 40%.

readingSections.title: Successive Profit Or Loss
readingSections.content:
The concept of successive change is used when an item is sold multiple times in a sequence at some profit or loss.

**For example:** If an item is first sold at a profit of, say, 20%, and then the same item is sold again at a loss of, say, 15%, the overall profit or loss is not simply $20\% - 15\% = 5\%$. Instead, the successive percentage changes are applied one after the other.

readingSections.title: Let’s take an example. Suppose the initial price of the item is Rs.100.
readingSections.content:
1. After a 20% profit, the selling price becomes Rs.100 + 20% of Rs.100 = Rs.120.
2. Now, if this item is sold again at a 15% loss, the new selling price becomes Rs.120 - 15% of Rs.120 = Rs.102.

So, even though there was a 20% profit followed by a 15% loss, the final selling price (Rs.102) is still higher than the initial price (Rs.100). This shows a net profit of 2%, not a net profit of 5% as one might initially think by simply subtracting the percentages.

For solving this type of question all concepts can be used which is already introduced in percentage.

readingSections.title: By Formula
readingSections.content:
In the case of multiple successive profits or losses, the selling price (SP) can be calculated by multiplying the cost price (CP) with the factors representing each profit or loss.

For multiple profits: SP = CP × (100 + P₁) % × (100 + P₂) % × (100 + P₃) % × ...

For multiple losses: SP = CP × (100 - L₁) % × (100 - L₂) % × (100 - L₃) % × ...

For a mix of profits and losses: SP = CP × (100 - L₁) % × (100 + P₂) % × (100 - L₃) % × ...

In these formulas, P represents profit percentages and L represents loss percentages.

readingSections.title: Example 17
readingSections.content:
Amit bought a bicycle for Rs 1000 and sold it to Raman at a profit of 20%. Then, Raman sold it to Kuldeep at a loss of 25%. Finally, Kuldeep sold it to Radhika at a profit of 60%. Then find overall profit and loss in the whole process.

### Solution

Method 1: Amit sold the bicycle to Raman at a 20% profit. So, the selling price becomes Rs. 1000 + 20% of Rs. 1000 = Rs. 1200.

Raman then sold the bicycle to Kuldeep at a 25% loss. So, the selling price becomes Rs 1200 - 25% of Rs 1200 = Rs 900.

Finally, Kuldeep sold the bicycle to Radhika at a 60% profit. So, the selling price becomes Rs 900 + 60% of Rs 900 = Rs 1440.

So, the overall selling price (Rs 1440) is higher than the initial buying price (Rs 1000).

The total profit is Rs 1440 - Rs 1000 = Rs 440.

Method 2: Profit percentage, P₁ = 20%, Loss percentage, L₂ = 25%, Profit percentage, P₃ = 60%, Cost price, CP = Rs 1000

The selling price (SP) is calculated as follows:

SP = CP × (100 + P1) % × (100 - L2) % × (100 + P3) %

SP = 1000 × (100 + 20)% × (100 - 25)% × (100 + 60) % = 1000 × 120% × 75% × 160%

SP = 1000 × (6/5) × (3/4) × (8/5) = 1440

The profit is then calculated by subtracting the cost price from the selling price:

Profit = SP - CP = Rs 1440 - Rs 1000 = Rs 440

So, the profit made is Rs 440.

Method 3: By Ratio: Profit percentage, P₁ = 20% = 1/5, so CP = 5 units and P = 1 unit.

Therefore, SP = CP + P = 5 units + 1 unit = 6 units.

Loss percentage, L₂ = 25% = 1/4, so CP = 4 units and L = 1 unit.

Therefore, SP = CP - L = 4 units - 1 unit = 3 units.

Profit percentage, P₃ = 60% = 3/5, so CP = 5 units and P = 3 units.

Therefore, SP = CP + P = 5 units + 3 units = 8 units.

The ratio of cost price to selling price is calculated as follows:

CP: SP = (5 × 4 × 5) : (6 × 3 × 8) = 25 : 36

The profit is then calculated by subtracting the cost price from the selling price:

P (in units) = SP - CP = 36 units - 25 units = 11 units

Given that the cost price is Rs.1000, the profit in rupees is calculated as follows:

Profit (in Rs) = Rs.1000 × (11/25) = Rs.440

So, the profit made is Rs.440.

Profit = 1440 - 1000 = 440

readingSections.title: In Case of Dishonest Shopkeeper
readingSections.content:
Case 1: When a shopkeeper commits to selling his goods at a cost price but provides less weight, there are three types of weights to consider: true weight, false weight, and error.

- True Weight: The true weight is the original weight that the customer intends to buy. This is the accurate measure of the goods that the customer expects to receive.
- False Weight: The false weight is the weight that the shopkeeper gives to the customer. This is usually less than the true weight, indicating that the shopkeeper is providing less than what was agreed upon.
- Error: The error is the difference between the true weight and the false weight. This represents the discrepancy in the weight provided by the shopkeeper compared to what the customer intended to purchase.

For Example, in a transaction where a customer intends to buy 10 kg of mangoes but receives only 9 kg, the true weight is 10 kg, the false weight is 9 kg, and the error is 1 kg.

98

Error=True Weight-False Weight

$$\text{In this case Profit \%} = \frac{\text{Error}}{\text{True weight} - \text{Error}} \times 100\%$$

When we calculate profit or loss percentage in case of quantity (not in terms of rupees.)

$$= \frac{\text{profit or loss in quantity}}{\text{quantity going out of shop}} \times 100$$

readingSections.title: Example 18
readingSections.content:
A dishonest dealer claims to sell his goods at cost price, but instead of using 1 kg, he uses 750 gm. and then finds his profit percentage.

### Solution

The dealer claims to sell 1 kg of goods, but he sells only 750 g.

Error = True Weight - False Weight = 1000 g - 750 g = 250 g

Now, we can calculate the profit percentage using the formula:

$$\text{Profit \%} = \frac{\text{Error}}{\text{True weight} - \text{Error}} \times 100\%$$

$$= \frac{250}{1000 - 250} \times 100\% = \frac{250}{750} \times 100\% = 33.33\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 19
readingSections.content:
A dishonest dealer claims to sell his goods at cost price, but cheats 20% by weight during selling the article then find his profit percentage.

### Solution

Method 1: The dealer claims to sell 100 gm of goods, but he sells only 80 gm (because he cheats 20% by weight). So, the error is the difference between these two weights.

Error = True Weight - False; Weight = 100 gm - 80 gm = 20 gm

Now, we can calculate the profit percentage using the formula:

$$\text{Profit \%} = \frac{\text{Error}}{\text{True weight} - \text{Error}} \times 100\%$$

$$= \frac{20}{100 - 20} \times 100\% = \frac{20}{80} \times 100\% = 25\%$$

### Method 2

Short Trick: When calculating profit, replace the denominator of the fraction with the difference between the numerator and the denominator. Then, convert this value into a percentage.

With a fraction of 20% = $\frac{1}{5}$,

The difference between the denominator and the numerator is 5 - 1=4

$$\text{So, profit \%} = \frac{1}{4} \times 100\% = 25\%$$

Case 2: When a shopkeeper manipulates the weight during both buying and selling and promises to sell goods at cost price, the profit percentage can be calculated as follows:

If the shopkeeper cheats by 'x%' while purchasing an item and by 'y%' during selling (by weight), then the profit percentage can be calculated using the following formula:

$$\text{Profit\%} = \frac{(x + y)}{(100 - y)} \times 100\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 20
readingSections.content:
A dishonest dealer cheats 60% in buying goods as well as 20% in selling goods by weight. What is his profit?

### Solution

### Method 1

$$x = 60\% \text{ and } y = 20\%$$

$$\text{Profit\%} = \frac{(x + y)}{(100 - y)} \times 100\%$$

$$\text{Profit\%} = \frac{(60 + 20)}{(100 - 20)} \times 100\% = 100\%$$

### Method 2

At the time of purchase use = pay for 100 grams and get 160 grams

At the time of sell use = receives for 100 grams and gives 80 grams

$$\text{Profit \%} = \frac{160 - 80}{80} \times 100 = 100\%$$

Case 3: When a shopkeeper manipulates weights and gains a certain percentage (a %), and also gains b% by selling the article for more than the cost price, then the

$$\text{Overall profit percent} = \left( a + b + \frac{ab}{100} \right) \%$$

readingSections.title: Example 21
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper purchases an article for Rs 600 and sells it for Rs 750. Additionally, he cheats by 20% while purchasing the article and by 25% while selling the article. Find his overall profit percentage

### Solution

### Method 1

Profit% by weight=a%

$$= \frac{(x + y)}{(100 - y)} \times 100\% = \frac{(20 + 25)}{(100 - 25)} \times 100\% = 60\%$$

$$\text{CP} = 600, \text{ SP} = 750 \text{ profit \%} = b\%$$

99

$$= \frac{(SP - CP)}{CP} \times 100\% = \frac{150}{600} \times 100\% = 25\%$$

Overall profit % = $\left(a + b + \frac{ab}{100}\right)\%$

$$= \left(60 + 25 + \frac{60 \times 25}{100}\right)\% = 100\%$$

### Method 2

Get 1200 gram instead of 1kg

Give 750 gram instead of 1kg

Profit% in volume = $\{(120 - 75) / 75\} \times 100 = 60\%$

Profit% in rupee = $\{(750 - 600) / 600\} \times 100 = 25\%$

Then use $a + b + \frac{a \times b}{100}$

Total profit % = $60 + 25 + \frac{60 \times 25}{100} = 85 + 15 = 100\%$

readingSections.title: Example 22
readingSections.content:
Ankita incurs a loss of 40% on selling groceries. However, while buying and selling, she cheats by weight, getting 40% more when buying and giving 20% less when selling. What is her overall profit or loss percentage?

### Solution

### Method 1

Profit% by weight:

$$\frac{(x + y)}{(100 - y)} \times 100\% = \frac{(40 + 20)}{(100 - 20)} \times 100\% = 75\%$$

b% = - 40%

The overall profit % = $\left(a + b + \frac{ab}{100}\right)\%$

Overall profit % = $\left(75 - 40 + \frac{75 \times (-40)}{100}\right)\% = 5\%$

(Because 5% is +ve)

So, Ankita has an overall profit of 5%.

### Method 2

Get 1400 gram instead of 1kg

Give 800 gram instead of 1kg

Profit% in volume $\frac{1400 - 800}{800} \times 100 = 75\%$

Loss% in rupee = 40 %

Then use $a + b + \frac{a \times b}{100}$

Total profit or loss % = $75 - 40 + \frac{75 \times (-40)}{100} = 35 - 30 = + 5\%$

readingSections.title: Concept 7
readingSections.content:
When percentage of profit and loss is increased or decreased and Selling price is increased or decreased then,

Just calculate the difference in the percentage of profit/loss and then percentage is equal to the Selling price changed.

readingSections.title: Example 23
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper sells his goods at 6 % profit. Had he sold it Rs. 2160 more than he would have gained 15% profit. Find the initial cost price?

### Solution

### Method 1

Let initial C.P. be 100

Initial S.P. $100 + 6\%$ of $100 = 106$

After attains profit 15% new S.P. $100 + 15\%$ of $100 = 115$

Difference between final and initial S.P. is $115 - 106 = 9$ ratio

1 ratio = $\frac{2160}{9} = 240$

Initial C.P. 100 ratio = $240 \times 100 = 24000$ Rs.

### Method 2

And price is increased Rs. 2160

So 9% = 2160

$$1\% = \frac{2160}{9} = 240$$

Initial C.P. (100) = $240 \times 100 = \text{Rs. } 24000$

A shopkeeper sells his goods at 14 % loss. Had he sold it Rs. 1440 more than he would gain 16 % profit. Find cost price?

readingSections.title: Concept 8
readingSections.content: When articles purchased and sold are not equal, We have to make them equal and then calculate profit and loss on the cost price and selling price.

readingSections.title: Example 26
readingSections.content:
A man purchases some articles at 11 articles for Rs. 10 and sells all the articles at 10 articles for Rs. 11. Find profit or loss percentage in the whole transaction?

### Solution

### Method 1

The man purchases 11 articles for Rs. 10. So, the cost price CP per article is $$\frac{10}{11}$$ Rs.

He sells 10 articles for Rs. 11. So, the selling price SP per article is $$\frac{11}{10}$$ Rs. The profit per article P is the selling price minus the cost price, $$P = SP - CP = \frac{11}{10} - \frac{10}{11}$$. To find the profit

percentage, we divide the profit per article by the cost price per article and multiply by 100, $$\text{Profit}\% = \frac{P}{CP} \times 100$$

Substituting the values we have,

$$\text{Profit}\% = \frac{\frac{11}{10} - \frac{10}{11}}{\frac{10}{11}} \times 100 = 21\%$$

### Method 2.

|  Quantity | Price | Because ATQ, number of articles are same  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  11 | 10 | Total C.P. = 10 × 10 = 100 (because according to question)  |
|  10 | 11 | Toal S.P. = 11 × 11 = 121  |

Then profit % = $$\frac{121 - 100}{100} \times 100 = 21\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 27
readingSections.content:
A man purchased some oranges at 1 orange for Rs. 2 and the same number of oranges at 2 oranges for Rs. 1 and sold all of them at 4 oranges for Rs. 3. Find profit or loss percentage?

### Solution

### Method 1

The man purchases some oranges at 1 orange for Rs. 2 and the same number of oranges at 2 oranges for Rs. 1.

So, the average cost price CP per orange is $$\left(\frac{2 + \frac{1}{2}}{2}\right) = \frac{5}{4}$$ Rs.

He sells all the oranges at 4 oranges for Rs. 3.

So, the selling price SP per orange is $$\frac{3}{4}$$ Rs. The loss per orange L is the cost price minus the selling price,

$$L = CP - SP = \frac{5}{4} - \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{2} \text{ Rs.}$$

$$\text{Loss}\% = \frac{L}{CP} \times 100$$

Substituting the values we have, $$\text{Loss}\% = \frac{1/2}{5/4} \times 100 = 40\%$$

### Method 2

|  Quantity | : | Price | Q : P  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  (Orange) | : | (Rs.) |   |
|  Purchase 1 | : | 2) × 2 | 2 : 4  |
|  Purchase 2 | : | 1) × 1 | 2 : 1  |
|  Total |  |  | 4 : 5  |
|  It is given that both quantity are same |  | Selling | 4 : 3  |

101

We purchased 4 oranges in Rs. 5 and sell 4 oranges in Rs. 3.

$$\text{So, loss \%} = \left( \frac{5-3}{5} \right) \times 100 = 40\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 28
readingSections.content:
A man buys some oranges at the rate of 5 for rs. 1 and the same number of oranges at 4 for rs. 1. He sold all of them at 9 for rs. 2. During the whole transaction he incurs a loss of rs. 30. Find the number of articles that he purchased?

### Solution

### Method 1

readingSections.content:
When one person purchases a certain amount of articles in

a rupee at a loss and want to earn a profit then how many articles he will sell in a rupee.

readingSections.title: Example 29
readingSections.content:
A man purchased some oranges at 230 oranges for Rs.1. How many for a rupee did he sell to gain 15%?

### Solution

### Method 1

The man initially buys oranges at a rate of 230 oranges for Rs.1. So, the cost price of each orange is Rs. $\frac{1}{230}$.

He wants to gain a profit of 15%. This means the selling price of each orange should be 115% of the cost price. Therefore,

$$\text{the selling price of each orange is } 1.15 \times (\text{Rs. } \frac{1}{230}) = \text{Rs. } \frac{1.15}{230}.$$

Hence, he sells 1 for Rs. $\frac{1.15}{230}$

$$= \frac{230}{1.15} \text{ oranges for Rs.1 to gain a profit of 15\%.}$$

So, the man sells 200 oranges for Rs.1 to gain a profit of 15%

### Method 2

Man wants a profit of 15% = $15/100 = 3/20$ i.e. if CP=20 Profit=3 & SP=23

Relation of CP : SP is inversely proportional to quantity purchased and sell

So, C.P. : S.P. = 20 : 23

Number of Oranges purchased : sell = 23 : 20

So, 23 ratio = 230 then 1 ratio = 10

So Number of Oranges sell 20 ratio = $20 \times 10$

$$= 200$$

readingSections.title: Example 30
readingSections.content:
By selling 12 oranges for a rupee a man loses 20%. How many for a rupee did he sell to earn 20% profit?

### Solution

### Method 1

The man initially sells 12 oranges for Rs.1 and incurs a loss of 20%. This means the cost price of 12 oranges is Rs.1/0.8 = Rs.1.25. So, the cost price of each orange is Rs.1.25/12.

Now, he wants to gain a profit of 20%. This means the selling price of each orange should be 120% of the cost price.

Therefore, the selling price of each orange is $1.2 \times \frac{1.25}{12} = \text{Rs.}$
$\frac{1.5}{12}$. Hence, he sells 1 for Rs. $\frac{1.5}{12} = \frac{12}{1.5} = 8$ oranges for Rs. 1 to gain a profit of 20%.

So, the man sells 8 oranges for Rs. 1 to gain a profit of 20%.

### Method 2

Let price be 100 but due to loss of 20% cost price was 100-20 i.e. = 80

At the time of sell he wants profit 20% so selling price was 100+20 i.e. = 120

So the ratio of C.P. : S.P. = 80 : 120 = 2 : 3

Relation of CP : SP is inversely proportional to quantity purchased and sell

Quantity of oranges purchased and sell are in the ratio of 3 : 2

3 ratio = 12 oranges i.e. 1 ratio = 4 oranges

Oranges will be sell 2 ratio = 2 × 4 = 8 oranges.

readingSections.title: Concept 10
readingSections.content: When a businessman sells parts of his goods in different types of profit or loss percentage then we have to compare them with total profit or loss percentage

readingSections.title: Example 31
readingSections.content:
A man purchases some number of articles at Rs. 5400 and he sells $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{rd}$ of them at 5% profit. At what profit % did he sell the remaining to gain 13% overall.

### Solution

### Method 1

$$2/3^{\text{rd}} \text{ part of } 5400 = \frac{2}{3} \times 5400 = \text{Rs. } 3600$$

Profit = 5% of 3600 = Rs. 180

Total profit 13% of 5400 = Rs. 702

So the remaining profit i.e. = 702 - 180 = Rs. 522

$$\text{So profit on } 5400 - 3600 \text{ will be } = \frac{522}{1800} \times 100 = 29\%$$

### Method 2

![Book diagram, page 103](/content-assets/ssc-cgl/quant-book/ocr-p103-img-26.jpeg)

### Method 3

Assume total part is 3 out of which

2 parts is at profit of 5% = 2 × 5 = 10%

Total i.e. 3 part is sell at a profit of 13% = 39%

Remaining profit is 39% - 10% = 29%

So the remaining articles will be sell on 29% profit.

readingSections.title: Example 32
readingSections.content:
A man purchases some number of articles at Rs. 18900 and he sells 3/8$^{th}$ of them at 12% profit. At what Loss % did he sell the remaining to gain 4% overall.

### Solution

Assume total part is 8 out of which

3 parts is at profit of 12% = 3 × 12% = 36%

Total i.e. 8 part is sell at a profit of 4% = 32%

So the 5 part of articles will be sell on the loss of 36% - 32% = 4%

$$\text{Loss percentage is equal to } \frac{4}{100} \times 5 = 0.80\%$$

readingSections.title: Concept 11
readingSections.content: When two articles are sold one at profit other at loss and the selling price of both articles are the same.

readingSections.title: Example 33
readingSections.content:
Ram sells a house at a profit of 20% and a horse at a loss of 25% but the selling price of both are the same. Then find the profit or loss % of Ram in the whole transaction?

### Solution

$$\text{House at a profit of } 20\% = \frac{20}{100} = \frac{1}{5}$$
CP=5

Profit=1

$$SP = 5 + 1 = 6$$

$$\text{Horse at a loss of } 25\% = \frac{25}{100} = \frac{1}{4}$$
CP=4

Loss=1

$$SP = 4 - 1 = 3$$

If we equalize both the SP

$$(SP : CP)_{\text{House}} = 6 : 5$$

$$(SP : CP)_{\text{Horse}} = (3 : 4) \times 2 = 6 : 8$$

Total CP of House and Horse = 5 + 8 = 13 &

Total SP of House and Horse = 6 + 6 = 12

$$\text{So loss percentage} = \frac{13 - 12}{13} \times 100 = \frac{1}{13} \times 100 = 7\frac{9}{13}\%$$

Chapter
11
DISCOUNT
Marked price:
The marked price, also known as the retail price or list price, is the
original price that a seller sets for a product or service. This price
is usually displayed on the product’s label or in a catalogue and is
represented by the abbreviation MP. When a discount is offered,
the marked price is often considered as 100% because it serves as
the base value for calculating the discount.
Discount:
A discount signifies a reduction in the original cost of a product
or service. It’s the difference between the marked price (the
price displayed on the product or listed in a catalogue) and
the selling price (the actual price at which the product is sold
after all discounts have been applied). It is generally denoted
by “D”.
Here’s how you can compute the discount:
Discount (D) = Marked Price (MP) - Selling Price (SP)
Concept:
Relation Between Marked Price And Selling Price
The discount rate is typically represented as a percentage.
Here’s how you can calculate it:
D
D% = × 100%
MP
MP − SP
D% = × 100%
MP
SP= MP (100-D) %
Substituting the given values:
500 − 480
Discount Percentage= × 100% =4%
500
So, Raman gave a discount of 4% on the toy.
Concept:
Type Of Discount
1. Flat Discount: A discount where the total discount is
given all at once.

Concept:
Relation Between Cost Price And Marked Price
The formula SP = CP × (100 + P/L)% is used when you know
the cost price (CP) and the profit or loss (P/L). If it’s a profit,
P is positive; if it’s a loss, L is negative.
The formula SP = MP × (100 - D) % is used when you know
the market price (MP) and the discount (D).
When you equate these two to find a relationship between CP,
MP, P/L, and D, you get
CP × (100 ± P/L) % = MP × (100 - D)%
In the case where profit/loss percentages (P1/L1 and P2/
L2) are given for two different conditions, and CP & MP are
fixed, then the relation will be
100 ± P 1/ L 1 100 − D 1
=
100 ± P 2 / L 2 100 − D 2

Concept:
If an item is given for free, then the price of the free article is also
considered as a discount. For example, if a book is purchased
for Rs 500 and a pen worth Rs 25 is given for free, then Rs 25
will be considered as a discount. Therefore, we can say that the
discount percentage is in concept (25 / 525) × 100 = 4 (16/21)
% or 4.76%

The marked price is 20% more than the cost price, so MP = 120% of CP = 120% of Rs 100 = Rs 120. Due to a discount of 25%, the selling price becomes SP = 75% of MP = 75% of Rs 120 = Rs 90. The loss is calculated as Loss = CP – SP = Rs 100 - Rs 90 = Rs 10.

readingSections.title: Marked price
readingSections.content:
The marked price, also known as the retail price or list price, is the original price that a seller sets for a product or service. This price is usually displayed on the product's label or in a catalogue and is represented by the abbreviation MP. When a discount is offered, the marked price is often considered as 100% because it serves as the base value for calculating the discount.

A discount signifies a reduction in the original cost of a product or service. It's the difference between the marked price (the price displayed on the product or listed in a catalogue) and the selling price (the actual price at which the product is sold after all discounts have been applied). It is generally denoted by "D".

Here's how you can compute the discount:

readingSections.title: Relation Between Marked Price And Selling Price
readingSections.content:
The discount rate is typically represented as a percentage. Here's how you can calculate it:

$$D\% = \frac{D}{MP} \times 100\%$$

$$D\% = \frac{MP - SP}{MP} \times 100\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 1
readingSections.content:
Raman printed a price of Rs 500 on a toy for sale, but after bargaining with the customer, he had to sell it at Rs 480. Find his discount percentage.

### Solution

Discount Percentage

$$= \frac{\text{Marked Price} - \text{Selling Price}}{\text{Marked Price}} \times 100\%$$

Substituting the given values:

$$\text{Discount Percentage} = \frac{500 - 480}{500} \times 100\% = 4\%$$

So, Raman gave a discount of 4% on the toy.

readingSections.title: Type Of Discount
readingSections.content: 1. **Flat Discount:** A discount where the total discount is given all at once.

readingSections.title: Example 2
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper has marked the price of a laptop as Rs 50,000. He offers a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is the selling price of the laptop after the discount?

### Solution

**Method 1:** Selling Price

= Marked Price (100-Discount) %

Substituting the given values:

$$\text{Selling Price} = 50000 \times (100 - 15) \% = 50000 \times \frac{85}{100} = \text{Rs } 42500$$

So, the selling price of the laptop after a discount of 15% is Rs 42,500.

**Method 2:** Short trick: Discount = 15% = $\frac{3}{20}$

Marked Price (base value for discount) = 20 units

Discount = 3 units

Therefore, the Selling Price is calculated as follows:

Selling Price = Marked Price - Discount

Selling Price = 20 units - 3 units = 17 units

If the Marked Price is Rs 50,000, then the Selling Price would be:

$$\text{Selling Price} = \frac{\text{Rs } 50000}{20 \text{ units}} \times 17 \text{ units}$$

Selling Price = Rs 42,500

2. Successive discount: A discount which is not given at once, but partially over more than one instance. For example, if a shopkeeper wants to give a 60% discount, but he gives it in two parts, that is 40% + 20%, then it will be called a successive discount. In the case of successive discounts, the total discount is less than a flat discount, even if the total discount percentage is the same.
3. Net Discount: The total effect of successive discounts is referred to as the net discount.

The net discount percentage is calculated as follows:

$$\text{Net discount \%} = \left(-D1 - D2 + \frac{D1 \times D2}{100}\right)\%$$

Here, D1 and D2 represent the discounts in percentage in two different cases.

The relationship between the selling price (SP) and the marked price (MP) in the case of more than one discount (D1, D2, D3, etc.) is given by:

$$\begin{array}{l} \text{SP} = \text{MP} \times (100 - \text{D1}) \% \times (100 - \text{D2}) \% \times (100 - \text{D3}) \\ \% \times \dots \end{array}$$

readingSections.title: Example 3
readingSections.content:
If a salesman offers two successive discounts of 30% and 20% on an article, what is the net discount on the article?

### Solution

Method 1: Net discount % = $$\left(-D1 - D2 + \frac{D1 \times D2}{100}\right)\%$$

Where D₁ and D₂ are the two successive discounts.

Given that D₁ = 30% and D₂ = 20%, we can substitute these values into the formula:

Net discount % = $$\left(-30 - 20 + \frac{(-30) \times (-20)}{100}\right)\%$$

$$= -30 - 20 + 6 = -44\%$$

So, the net discount offered on the article is 44%.

Method 2: For a discount of 30%, which is equivalent to $$\frac{3}{10}$$, the MP is 10 units and the SP is 10 - 3 = 7 units.

For a discount of 20%, which is equivalent to $$\frac{1}{5}$$, the MP is 5 units and the SP is 5 - 1 = 4 units.

The ratio of MP to SP is therefore (10 × 5) : (7 × 4) = 50 : 28, which simplifies to 25 : 14.

The combined discount percentage is then given by

$$\frac{25 - 14}{25} \times 100\% = 44\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 4
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, India, has a unique way of attracting customers. He offers three successive discounts on his products. The first discount

is 16.66%, the second is 66.66%, and the third is 40%. Calculate the net discount percentage offered by the shopkeeper after all the discounts have been applied.

### Solution

The first discount of 16.66% is equivalent to 1/6, so the marked price (MP) is 6 units and the selling price (SP) after the discount is 6 - 1 = 5 units.

The second discount of 66.66% is equivalent to 2/3, so the MP is 3 units and the SP after the discount is (3 - 2) = 1 unit.

The third discount of 40% is equivalent to $$\frac{2}{5}$$, so the MP is 5 units and the SP after the discount is (5 - 2) = 3 units.

The ratio of MP to SP for the combined discounts is therefore (6 × 3 × 5) : (5 × 1 × 3) = 90:15 = 6:1.

The combined discount percentage is then given by $$\frac{6 - 1}{6} \times 100\% = 83.33\%$$

readingSections.title: Relation Between Cost Price And Marked Price
readingSections.content:
The formula SP = CP × (100 ± P/L)% is used when you know the cost price (CP) and the profit or loss (P/L). If it's a profit, P is positive; if it's a loss, L is negative.

The formula SP = MP × (100 - D) % is used when you know the market price (MP) and the discount (D).

When you equate these two to find a relationship between CP, MP, P/L, and D, you get

$$\text{CP} \times (100 \pm \text{P/L}) \% = \text{MP} \times (100 - \text{D})\%$$

In the case where profit/loss percentages (P1/L1 and P2/L2) are given for two different conditions, and CP & MP are fixed, then the relation will be

$$\frac{100 \pm P1 / L1}{100 \pm P2 / L2} = \frac{100 - D1}{100 - D2}$$

readingSections.title: Example 5
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper sells a product at a discount of 40% and still manages to make a profit of 25% on its cost price. If the marked price of the product is Rs 800, what is the cost price of the product?

### Solution

The profit (P) is 25%.

The marked price (MP) is Rs 800.

The discount (D) is 40%.

$$\text{CP} \times (100 + \text{P}) \% = \text{MP} \times (100 - \text{D}) \%$$

We can rearrange the formula to solve for CP (Cost Price):

108

$$CP = MP \times \frac{(100 - D)\%}{(100 + P)\%} = 800 \times \frac{(100 - 40)\%}{(100 + 25)\%}$$

$$= 800 \times \frac{60\%}{125\%} = \text{Rs } 384$$

readingSections.title: Example 6
readingSections.content:
A retailer labels the price of his goods in such a way that after offering a discount of 15%, he still makes a profit of 25%. However, due to pressure from customers, he is forced to offer a discount of 31%. What is the net profit percentage for the retailer?

### Solution

Let's solve this problem using the given formula:

$$\frac{(100 + P_1)}{(100 + P_2)} = \frac{(100 - D_1)}{(100 - D_2)}$$

$$\frac{(100 + 25)}{(100 + P_2)} = \frac{(100 - 15)}{(100 - 31)}$$

**P$_{1}$=1.5% (Approx.)**

readingSections.title: Example 7
readingSections.content:
The original price of a car is Rs 50000. After three consecutive discounts, it is sold for Rs 37192.5. If the first discount is 10% and the second discount is 5%, what is the percentage of the third discount?

### Solution

The first discount of 10% is equivalent to $\frac{1}{10}$, so the marked price (MP) is 10 units, and the selling price (SP) after the discount is 10 - 1 = 9 units.

The second discount of 5% is equivalent to $\frac{1}{20}$, so the MP is 20 units, and the SP after the discount is 20 - 1 = 19 units.

Let's assume that the third discount is x% which is equivalent to $\frac{x}{100}$, so the MP is 100 units and the SP after the discount is 100 - x = (100-x) units.

The ratio of MP to SP for the combined discounts is therefore $(10 \times 20 \times 100) : (9 \times 19 \times (100-x))$.

Given that the original price of a car is Rs 50000 (which represents our total Marked Price) and it's sold for Rs 37192.5 (which represents our total Selling Price), we can set up the equation:

$$\frac{10 \times 20 \times 100}{9 \times 19 \times (100 - x)} = \frac{50000}{37192.5}$$

$$x = 13\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 8
readingSections.content:
The cost price of 15 pens is equal to the selling price of 10 pens, and the discount on 8 pens is equal to the profit on 6 pens. Can you calculate the difference between the profit percentage and the discount percentage?

### Solution

The cost price of 15 pens is equal to the selling price of 10 pens

$$So, CP : SP = 10 : 15 = 2 : 3$$

Discount on 8 pens is equal to the profit on 6 pens

$$So, P : D = 8 : 6 = 4 : 3$$

On equating the equation: $CP : SP : P : D : MP = 8 : 12 : 4 : 3 : 15$

$$\text{Profit } \% = \frac{4}{8} \times 100\% = 50\%$$

$$\text{Discount}\% = \frac{3}{15} \times 100\% = 20\%$$

So, the difference between the profit percentage and discount percentage is 50% - 20% = 30%

readingSections.title: Concept 4
readingSections.content: If an item is given for free, then the price of the free article is also considered as a discount. For example, if a book is purchased for Rs 500 and a pen worth Rs 25 is given for free, then Rs 25 will be considered as a discount. Therefore, we can say that the discount percentage is in concept $(25 / 525) \times 100 = 4 (16/21)$ % or 4.76%

readingSections.title: Example 9
readingSections.content:
Find the discount on buy 7 get 1 free.

### Solution

If the selling price (SP) of one article is Rs 1, then for 7 articles, the SP would be Rs 7. However, with the offer "buy 7 get 1 free", you're getting 8 articles for the price of 7.

So, it can be considered that MP = Rs 8 and SP = Rs 7 and Discount = Rs 1

$$\text{Discount } \% = \frac{\text{Discount}}{MP} \times 100\%$$

Substituting the values:

$$\text{Discount } \% = \frac{1}{8} \times 100\% = 12.5\%$$

readingSections.title: Example 10
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper offers a 25% discount on a chair and also includes a free table worth Rs 500. If the marked price of the chair is Rs 2500, then find the overall discount percentage.

### Solution

Discount given by shopkeeper = 25% of 2500 = Rs 625

Addition Gift worth = Rs 500

So total discount = 500+625=1125

Overall discount % = $$\frac{1125}{3000} \times 100 = 37\frac{1}{2}$$ or 37.5%

readingSections.title: Example 11
readingSections.content:
A shopkeeper printed Rs 60 on his article, gave a 15% discount and also gave a gift of Rs 3. After that, he earns a profit of 20% and then find his cost price.

### Solution

The shopkeeper has printed Rs 60 on the article, but he gives a 15% discount.

So, the selling price (SP) after discount will be:

$$\mathrm{SP} = 60 - \frac{15}{100} \times 60 = \mathrm{Rs} 51$$

He also gives a gift worth Rs 3. So, the effective selling price (ESP) becomes:

ESP = SP - Gift price = 51 - 3 = Rs 48

Given that the shopkeeper still makes a profit of 20%, we can set up the equation:

120% of Cost Price (CP) = Rs 48

So, CP=Rs 40

readingSections.title: Example 12
readingSections.content:
A dishonest trader marks up his goods by 20% and gives a discount of 25%. Besides, he gets 40% more amount per kg from the wholesaler and Sells 20% less per kg to the customer. What is the overall profit/loss percentage?

### Solution

### Method 1

Let the cost price of the goods be Rs 100.

The marked price is 20% more than the cost price, so MP = 120% of CP = 120% of Rs 100 = Rs 120.

Due to a discount of 25%, the selling price becomes SP = 75% of MP = 75% of Rs 120 = Rs 90.

The loss is calculated as Loss = CP - SP = Rs 100 - Rs 90 = Rs 10.

Therefore, Loss% = $$\frac{\text{Loss}}{CP} \times 100\%$$

= $$\frac{10}{100} \times 100\% = 10\%$$ (This will be negative in the net change formula because it's a loss)

The profit percentage by cheating is calculated as

Profit% by cheating = $$\frac{x + y}{100 - y} \times 100\%$$

= $$\frac{40 + 20}{100 - 20} \times 100\% = 75\%$$ (This will be positive in the net change formula because it's a profit)

The net profit percentage is calculated as Net profit %

$$= \left(a + b + \frac{ab}{100}\right)\%$$

$$= \left(-10 + 75 - \frac{10 \times 75}{100}\right) = 57.5\% \text{ profit.}$$

### Method 2

Total profit/loss = $$a + b + \frac{a \times b}{100}$$ (where profit is in positive and loss is in negative)

$$= -10 + 75 + \frac{(-10) \times 75}{100} = 57.50\%$$

+ indicates profit of 57.50%

readingSections.title: Chapter exercises
readingSections.content:
1. If a product was sold for Rs. 500 and has a Marked price of 600, what is the discount percentage?
(a) 16.66% (b) 15.33%
(c) 15.55% (d) 17.14%
2. If a product has a Marked price of 280 and a discount of 32%, what is the selling price?
(a) 144.4 (b) 185.4
(c) 190.4 (d) 195.4
3. If a salesman gives a discount on an article by 50% and then by 25%, what is the net discount on that article?
(a) 62.5% (b) 37.5%
(c) 75% (d) 25%
4. If a salesman gives a discount on an article by 10%, 20%, and 30% successively, what is the net discount on that article?
(a) 49.6 (b) 50.4
(c) 60 (d) 59.6
5. If a customer buys 5 items and gets 3 free, what is the discount per item?
(a) 12.5% (b) 37.5%
(c) 35.75% (d) 25%
6. If a customer buys 3 items and gets 2 free, and then gets an additional 25% discount, what is the equivalent single discount?
(a) 32% (b) 48%
(c) 68% (d) 55%
7. If a customer is given a discount of 55.55% on the marked price of an article and the selling price is 2800, what is the original marked price of the article?
(a) 6100 (b) 6700
(c) 6300 (d) 5600
8. If a customer is given a discount of 66.66% on the marked price of an article and the selling price is 108, what is the original marked price of the article?
(a) 216 (b) 312
(c) 54 (d) 324
9. If the marked price of a computer is Rs 49000 and after two successive discounts it is sold at Rs 35280, and if the first discount is 20%, What is the value of the second discount?
(a) 10% (b) 15%
(c) 28% (d) 8%
10. If a seller wants to gain 14% after giving a discount of 44% on an article, what should be the marked price if the cost price is Rs 784?
(a) 1544 (b) 1532
(c) 1596 (d) 1546
11. Rajesh marked a book for sale at a price of Rs 600. However, after bargaining with the customer, he had to sell it at Rs 540. What is his discount percentage?
(a) 8% (b) 10%
(c) 12% (d) 15%
12. A retailer has marked the price of a smartphone as Rs 30,000. He offers a discount of 20% on the marked price. What is the selling price of the smartphone after the discount?
(a) Rs 24,000 (b) Rs 25,000
(c) Rs 26,000 (d) Rs 27,000
13. If a store offers two successive discounts of 20% and 10% on a product, what is the net discount on the product?
(a) 28% (b) 30%
(c) 32% (d) 35%
14. A shopkeeper in Delhi, India, has a unique way of attracting customers. He offers three successive discounts on his products. The first discount is 10%, the second is 50%, and the third is 30%. What is the net discount percentage offered by the shopkeeper after all the discounts have been applied?
(a) 70% (b) 68.5%
(c) 74.5% (d) 76%
15. A retailer sells a product at a discount of 30% and still manages to make a profit of 20% on its cost price. If the marked price of the product is Rs 600, what is the cost price of the product?
(a) Rs 500 (b) Rs 350
(c) Rs 300 (d) Rs 450
16. A retailer labels the price of his goods in such a way that after offering a discount of 20%, he still makes a profit of 30%. However, due to pressure from customers, he is forced to offer a discount of 36%. What is the net profit percentage for the retailer?

(a) 4% (b) 5%
(c) 6% (d) 7%
17. The original price of a bike is Rs 70,000. After three consecutive discounts, it is sold for Rs 42,840. If the first discount is 15% and the second discount is 10%, what is the percentage of the third discount?
(a) 5% (b) 10%
(c) 15% (d) 20%
18. The cost price of 20 pens is equal to the selling price of 15 pens, and the discount on 10 pens is equal to the profit on 8 pens. Can you calculate the difference between the profit percentage and the discount percentage?
(a) 25% (b) 33.33%
(c) 16.66% (d) 50%
19. A dishonest trader marks up his goods by 30% and gives a discount of 20%. Besides, he gets 50% more amount per kg from the wholesaler and sells 30% less per kg to the customer. What is the overall profit percentage? (Approx)
(a) 122% (b) 120%
(c) 121% (d) 123%
20. A merchant buys a chair listed at Rs. 2,000 and gets successive discounts of 15% and 5%. What is the selling price of the chair?
(a) Rs. 1,675 (b) Rs. 2,115
(c) Rs. 2,400 (d) Rs. 1,615
21. A vendor marks his products 15% above his cost price. If he allows his customers a 15% discount on the marked price, does he make a profit or loss, if any?
(a) 2.25% loss
(b) 2.25% profit
(c) No profit no loss
(d) 5% profit
22. The marked price is 30% higher than the cost price. A discount of 25% is given on the marked price. By this type of sale, is there a profit or loss?
(a) 2.5% loss
(b) 2.5% profit
(c) No profit no loss
(d) 10% profit
23. A retailer buys 50 notebooks at the marked price of 45 notebooks from a wholesaler. If he sells these notebooks giving a discount of 2%, what is the profit percent?
(a) 8% (b) 9%
(c) 8.88% (d) 9.99%
24. A television is listed at Rs. 200 with a discount of 25%. What additional discount must be offered to the customer to bring the net price to Rs. 135?
(a) 5% (b) 10%
(c) 15% (d) 20%
25. If a shop-keeper marks his goods for a certain amount so as to get a 36% gain after allowing a discount of 15%, then his marked price is
(a) 115% of cost price
(b) 160% of cost price
(c) 125% of cost price
(d) 130% of cost price
26. A shopkeeper prints the price of his goods so that after giving a discount of 15% he can gain 36%, but after being persuaded by a customer he has to give a discount of 25%. What is the new profit percentage of the shopkeeper?
(a) 20% (b) 33%
(c) 23% (d) 25%
27. A and B sold the same article. The mark price of product is Rs.24000. A gives the discount 10% on the first 40% amount of marked up price and on remaining he gives 15% discount. B gives 15% discount on first Rs.20000 and 10% on remaining. What is the difference between their S.P.?
(a) 240 (b) 280
(c) 360 (d) 540
28. A shopkeeper buys 40 bicycles and marks them at 25% above the cost price. He allows a discount of 10% on the marked price for cash sales, and 5% for credit sales. If one – fourth of the stock is sold for credit and the rest for cash, and if the total profit be Rs.37125, what is the cost price of a bicycle?
(a) Rs.7000 (b) Rs.6500
(c) Rs.6200 (d) Rs.6600
29. The cost price of an article is Rs.42000. The shopkeeper offers a discount of 20% on it and loses at a rate half of the rate of discount rate. The marked price of the article is
(a) Rs.42000 (b) Rs.47250
(c) Rs.37800 (d) Rs.40500
30. A shopkeeper bought an article marked at Rs.22800 at two successive discounts of 15% and 20%. He spent Rs.1064 on transportation and sold the article for Rs.20710. What was the percentage of profit earned by the shopkeeper?
(a) 25% (b) 30%
(c) 35% (d) 20%

examples.text: Ramesh invests an unknown sum of money in a scheme that offers varying interest rates over time. The interest rate is 5% per annum for the first 2 years, 7% per annum for the subsequent 4 years, and 10% per annum for any years beyond the sixth year. Given that the total interest received = Rs. 61,200 (which corresponds to the total payable interest of 68%). 61200 × 100 P = Rs 90, 000 68

examples.text: Rahul invests a sum of money in a scheme that offers 5% interest per annum, with an increase of 1% per annum each year. If at the end of 3 years, he receives Rs. 12,960 as interest, what is the amount of money invested by Rahul? Solution: Let’s assume the invested amount is 100%. The scheme offers an interest rate of 5% per annum, which increases by 1% each year. So, the interest rates for the three years would be 5%, 6%, and 7%, respectively. examples.label: Example
examples.text: Ankit borrows a sum of money at the rate of 4% p.a. for the first 3 years, 8% p.a. for the next 2 years, and 10% p.a. beyond 5 years. At the end of 8 years, he pays a total amount of Rs. 18960. Find the amount of loan taken by Ankit. Solution: The invested money, P, is 100%. The interest for the first 3 years at 4% per annum is given by 3 × 4% = 12%. The interest for the next 2 years at 8% per annum is 2 × 8% = 16%. The interest for the last 3 years at 10% per annum is 3 × 10% = 30%. So, the total payable interest = 12% + 16% + 30% = 58%. Amount = 100%+58% = 158% 18960 Therefore, P = 158 × 100 = Rs 12, 000

examples.text: A sum of Rs. 3,000 amounts to Rs. 4,200 in 5 years at a certain rate of simple interest. If the rate of interest is increased by 2%, how much the same sum amounts in the same time. Solution: The sum will be increased by 2% for 5 years, so it will be 5 × 2%=10%. Therefore, the increased amount is 10% of Rs. 3,000= Rs. 300. So, the new amount is Rs. 4,200 + Rs. 300 = Rs. 4,500.
